body:
I'm nervous about us trying to delete an object at a pointer passed into the method here:
- If a programmer calls this method, and then later tries to reference `p_custom_header` after the method call, there's a possibility it may now be an invalid pointer (but notably not `nullptr`, so I don't think it can be checked for validity?)
- Alternatively, there may be the possibility that if a process expects this method to be called, but for some reason it isn't, then we could be left with a memory leak?

Overall I think it might be better to try and find a different way to control the lifecycle of this custom header. 

---

Thinking further about this, though, I recognize that this method is known to behave unusually (from before your PR), since it creates a "throwaway" tooltip. So, in this specific case, I think it's more reasonable for a programmer to assume that one way or another, the header they send into this method is going to end up becoming unusable. It might be good to get a more maintainer's and/or experienced contributor's opinions on this.

I recognize this is very nitpicky, but unless there's a particular reason to have this extra line here, it might be good to remove it just so that the PR's differences are minimal. (Maintainers or other contributors with more experience, feel free to veto this if you feel it's fine 😅)

As noted [below](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/123310/changes#r3963447098), I think it'd be better to make a subclass that you can create and populate an instance of for each warning. If you do this, then this method could move into that subclass. (Same is true for `_diagnostic_row_mouse_exited` and `_on_diagnostic_copy_pressed`.)
Like above, I recognize it's a tiny thing but it may be good to remove this newline for the sake of keeping the diff minimal, unless it feels like it significantly helps code readability

I believe this will be necessary to ensure that a stray `[` in a diagnostic message doesn't cause issues with the BBCode down the line:
```suggestion
		msg_label->append_text(vformat("[color=%s][b]%s[/b][/color] %s", color, title_text, p_msg.replace("[", "[lb]")));
```
Alternatively, you may be able to use [`push_color()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_richtextlabel.html#class-richtextlabel-method-push-color) and [`push_bold()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_richtextlabel.html#class-richtextlabel-method-push-bold) (along with [`pop()`](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_richtextlabel.html#class-richtextlabel-method-pop)) to avoid needing BBCode at all.

I think there should be a more efficient way to handle the mouse entering the overall area of the diagnostic box, than adding the pair of signals to all of its individual elements. Doing it this way can also cause the hover state of the box to get out of sync, allowing multiple copy buttons to display at once:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1b4cc713-bcda-435a-8f4c-8d7b2a872eaf

Thanks for pointing this out. I agree that deleting p_custom_header inside this method makes its ownership/lifetime less clear. I’ll look into a way to handle the header lifecycle without deleting a pointer passed into the method, while keeping the existing behavior of the throwaway tooltip intact.
I just added it when I was coding because I was getting lost I will remove it in the next commit.
Agreed. I’ll move these into the `DiagnosticItemRow` subclass so that each diagnostic row owns its hover and copy behavior, instead of keeping the callbacks in `ScriptTextEditor`.

Agreed. I’ll replace the lambda with a `DiagnosticItemRow` subclass and create/populate one row for each diagnostic as suggested. This also lets the diagnostic-specific behavior stay within the row itself.

Good point. I’ll handle the diagnostic message separately from the BBCode formatting so characters like [ in the message can’t be interpreted as BBCode. I’ll use the `push_color()/push_bold()` approach if it fits cleanly; otherwise I’ll escape the message before appending it.

I’ll move the hover handling into `DiagnosticItemRow` and handle the hover state from the row itself, rather than connecting the same signals to every child. This should also prevent multiple copy buttons from getting stuck visible.

Right now make_tooltip() can still memdelete a pointer that was passed in (the !p_target case, and the "can't show a tooltip right now" case). I tightened it up a bit so the one caller we have basically never hits that path anymore, but that's just avoiding the problem in practice, not actually fixing the ownership issue.

A few ways I could take this, honestly not sure which you'd prefer:

1. Just document it clearly say straight up in the comment that `make_tooltip` takes ownership of the header and you can't touch it after calling. Smallest change, doesn't fix the underlying weirdness but at least it's not a surprise anymore.
2. Never delete something we didn't create if we can't use the header, just error out instead of freeing it, and make the caller responsible for checking beforehand if it's worth building one at all.
3. Bigger refactor don't pass a pointer in at all, have make_tooltip build the header itself once it knows it's actually going to use it.

I lean toward just doing - 1 for now since this method's always had a kind of weird lifecycle anyway (the whole throwaway tooltip thing), and doing - 2 or - 3 as a bigger followup if it ever comes up again elsewhere. But this is really your call as the one who flagged it what do you think makes the most sense here?
The class definition should be moved into a header file, with the methods (at least ones with significant bodies) defined in the cpp file.


Is there a need to convert the theme color as a `Color` into an HTML color string, then back into a `Color`? Or could you just store the value from `get_theme_color()` as a `Color`?
I think for now I agree with going with approach 1. The way the method works overall is unusual, but this behavior seems to go along with it.

Is there a reason `real_t` is being used here instead of `float`? I'm used to seeing the latter in the Godot codebase, although I'm not sure how much of a hard rule that is.

---

I can see that by searching `real_t` in the `editor` folder, there are many other instances of it being used in place of `float` already. So this may be a non-issue actually 😅

It should only be `real_t` if it's directly relevant for precision computations or fed to a precision sensitive type I'd say, otherwise it risks creating inconsistencies. `real_t` is based on the precision of the build and used in `Vector2/3/4` and the other math types. Generally you should stick to either `float` or `double` depending on the precision needs of the code and not use `real_t` directly unless it should be affected by the double/single precision build option

tl;dr; generally only use `real_t` inside the core math types and related code, or when it is meant to be fed into those types

Thank you very much for the clarification! That makes sense, but I didn't see it mentioned on [the contribution docs's "C++ rules and guidelines" page](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/engine/guidelines/cpp_usage_guidelines.html#), or any mention of `real_t` in the contributing docs for that matter. The behavior you described is somewhat mentioned in the ["Physics > Large world coordinates" section of the manual](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/physics/large_world_coordinates.html#known-incompatibilities) but there it is specifically in the context of GDExtension.

Do you think a more thorough description of this `real_t` behavior would make sense to add to the "C++ rules and guidelines" page (or another page) so it is available for quick reference, like how disallowed features already are?
(This question sparked that exact conversation already and we're looking at it!)

@AThousandShips I used `real_t` here because I thought it would be preferable for preserving precision, but I wasn't aware of the drawbacks of using it outside of precision-sensitive code. Now that I understand the distinction better, what do you think would be more appropriate for these particular calculations? Since these values come from `get_global_position()` and are only being used for bounds/position checks, should I change them to `float`, or would keeping `real_t` be appropriate here?
I think `float` is best, if precision matters it should be changed to `double` but IMO not `real_t`

I was testing it out To fix the flickering issue when moving between the rows, I removed the `VBoxContainer` separation and instead wrapped each row in a `MarginContainer`. This makes the hover hitboxes physically touch in the exact midpoint between the text, completely eliminating the dead zone!

It now achieves the exact same smooth hover behavior without needing any process polling or manual hit detection math.
